period: New Kingdom statues, mostly 18th Dynasty; buried probably in the Roman period; found 1989
summary: In 1989 a routine check of the ground under Luxor Temple turned up a pit of near-perfect statues buried by priests; the king on his sledge is the star.
look: A hall built for the statues found in 1989 under the sun court of Amenhotep III at Luxor Temple. The tallest is Amenhotep III in red quartzite, about 2.5 m high, standing on a sledge. Around him are gods, goddesses and kings, including Horemheb kneeling before the god Atum, Hathor, and Iunyt, a local goddess of Armant.
story:
In 1989 Egyptian workers were testing the ground beneath the sun court of Amenhotep III at Luxor Temple, checking the foundations, when they broke into a pit. Inside, laid down with care, were statues: 26 came out, many in near-perfect condition.

Why were they buried? A statue in a temple was sacred; you could not simply throw away the image of a god or a king. When priests needed space, they buried such statues in holy ground, as they did on a far bigger scale in the Karnak cachette. The most likely moment here is the Roman period: around 300 AD Diocletian turned Luxor Temple into the heart of a legionary fortress, and the old cult was squeezed into a corner. Burying the statues may have protected them, or simply made room.

The centrepiece shows Amenhotep III in red quartzite, wearing the double crown and standing on a sledge. The sledge is the clue. This is not just a portrait: it is the king as a divine image, a cult statue to be dragged in procession and worshipped, fitting for a temple devoted to the king's divine ka. Nearby, Horemheb, the general who became the last king of the dynasty, kneels before Atum, the creator. Iunyt was a goddess of Armant, just south of Thebes. Another figure of Amun is thought to carry the features of Tutankhamun: kings liked to lend their faces to gods.
details: Amenhotep III on his sledge: red quartzite, about 2.5 m tall. Look down at the runners under his feet.
Horemheb kneeling before Atum: the general turned king, presenting offerings to the creator god.
Look for Hathor and Iunyt: goddesses who spent many centuries in the dark under the temple court.
Surfaces: buried in sand, these statues kept crisp detail that statues left standing outside lost.
At Luxor Temple today, find the sun court of Amenhotep III: the pit was under its floor.
fun_fact: The discovery was an accident of engineering: the workers were only checking the soil under the court, and found a pit of kings and gods.
narration: This hall was built for one discovery. In 1989 Egyptian workers were testing the ground beneath the sun court of Amenhotep the Third at Luxor Temple, checking the foundations, when they broke into a pit full of statues. Twenty-six came out, many in near-perfect condition. They had been buried on purpose. A statue in a temple was sacred: you could not throw away the image of a god or a king. When space was needed, priests buried them in holy ground. The most likely moment is the Roman period, when around 300 AD the emperor Diocletian turned Luxor Temple into a fortress for his legion. The star is Amenhotep the Third in red quartzite, about two and a half metres tall, wearing the double crown and standing on a sledge. That sledge is the key. This is not just a portrait of the king, it is the king as a divine image, to be dragged in procession and worshipped. Around him stand gods and goddesses, including Hathor and Iunyt, a local goddess of Armant, and Horemheb, the general who became king, kneeling before the creator god Atum. At Luxor Temple, stand in the court where they were found. For now, walk round Amenhotep, and look down at the runners of the sledge beneath his feet.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Akhenaten, c. 1350 BC
summary: Akhenaten's lost temple at Karnak, rebuilt from small blocks his successors used as rubble: palace life, workshops and the royal couple under the sun's hands.
look: A long wall of small painted sandstone blocks, 283 of them, reassembled along the gallery. The colours survive in places. Read it in bands: the Aten disc with its rays ending in hands, the royal couple offering, and below them storerooms, workshops and people at work. Colossal sandstone heads of Akhenaten nearby show his long face.
story:
Early in his reign, before he founded his new city at Amarna, Amenhotep IV, soon to call himself Akhenaten, built temples to the Aten, the sun disc, at Karnak. To build fast he used talatat: standard blocks about 27 by 27 by 54 cm, half a cubit by half a cubit by one, light enough for one man to carry.

After his death his religion was abandoned and his name cursed. Horemheb and the Ramesside kings pulled down his temples and used the blocks as fill and foundations at Karnak, inside pylons such as the Ninth and under the Hypostyle Hall. Inside the pylons the paint survived. Tens of thousands of talatat have been recovered. From the 1960s the Akhenaten Temple Project photographed them and used computers to help match scenes, one of the first such uses in archaeology. This wall is one of the results.

The scenes break with everything before them. The king and Nefertiti offer to the Aten, whose rays end in little hands holding the sign of life to their faces. Below, the life of the temple and palace: storerooms stacked with jars, bakers, brewers, workmen, servants. The figures are loose and lively, the bodies stretched in the Amarna style.

The colossal heads nearby come from statues of Akhenaten at Karnak: the long chin, the full lips, the narrow slanting eyes. Whether that face was a portrait, a style or a statement of religion is still argued.
details: Find the Aten: a disc whose rays end in little hands, some holding an ankh to the royal faces.
Look for Nefertiti offering alongside the king: she appears in these scenes as an active partner.
Lower rows: storerooms of jars, bakers and brewers, everyday work in Akhenaten's temple.
Size up one block: each is about three hand-spans long, a load one man could carry alone.
The sandstone heads of Akhenaten: long chin, full lips and narrow slanting eyes.
fun_fact: Talatat may simply mean 'threes': one theory says Egyptian workmen named the blocks because each is about three hand-spans long.
narration: This long painted wall was rebuilt from 283 small blocks taken out of Karnak's pylons. They come from temples that Akhenaten, the heretic king, built to the Aten, the sun disc, at Karnak about 1350 BC, before he left Thebes for his new city at Amarna. To build fast he used standard little blocks, each about three hand-spans long, light enough for one man to carry. Archaeologists call them talatat. When Akhenaten died, his religion was abandoned and his name cursed. Later kings pulled down his temples and packed the blocks inside their own pylons as rubble, among them Karnak's Ninth Pylon. That insult turned out to be lucky: inside the pylons, the paint survived. Tens of thousands of these blocks have been found, and in the 1960s a project began to photograph them and match them like a giant jigsaw, one of the first uses of computers in archaeology. Look at the top. The Aten is a disc whose rays end in little hands, holding the sign of life to the faces of the king and Nefertiti. Lower down, the life of the temple: storerooms full of jars, bakers, brewers, people at work. Nearby stand colossal heads of Akhenaten from the same temples. Find a ray ending in a hand, and follow it down to a royal face.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Tutankhamun, c. 1323 BC
summary: A gilded cow's head from Tutankhamun's treasury: the celestial cow who lifted the sun into the sky, one of the few pieces of his tomb kept in Luxor.
look: A cow's head of gilded wood, with dark horns and inlaid eyes, made for Tutankhamun's tomb, KV62. The Grand Egyptian Museum has been gathering the king's whole treasure, so if it is not on display, that is probably where it went; trust the labels for what is still here.
story:
Mehet-Weret, 'the Great Flood', was the celestial cow: a goddess of water, creation and rebirth who lifted the newborn sun into the sky every day, carrying it between her horns. In the Book of the Dead she is credited with the birth of Ra, and she helps the dead reach the afterlife. A cow who carries the sun up out of the dark was exactly what a dead king needed. She overlaps with Hathor, and labels often use both names.

The head was found in the Treasury of KV62, the small room beyond the burial chamber that Howard Carter cleared after the coffins. Almost all of Tutankhamun's objects went to the Egyptian Museum in Cairo and are now at the Grand Egyptian Museum, which you visited on 11 October. A handful were kept in Luxor, near the tomb itself.

One of the three ritual beds from the tomb is shaped as the same celestial cow, with lyre-shaped horns and a sun disc between them. If you saw it at GEM, this head is its small sister.
details: The horns: curved like a lyre, the cradle for the sun the celestial cow lifted into the sky.
The gilding: a thin skin of gold over carved wood, the technique used for most of the tomb's furniture.
Look for other Tutankhamun pieces nearby: labels will say KV62 or 'tomb of Tutankhamun'.
Compare it in memory with the cow-headed ritual bed at GEM: same goddess, same lyre horns.
fun_fact: Her name means 'Great Flood', and one scholar links her to the Milky Way, a river of stars flowing across the night sky.
narration: This golden cow's head comes from the tomb of Tutankhamun, K V 62. It shows Mehet Weret, whose name means the Great Flood: the celestial cow who lifted the newborn sun into the sky between her horns. For a dead king that was the right companion, a goddess who carries the sun up out of the darkness every morning. In the Book of the Dead she is credited with the birth of the sun god, and she helps the dead reach the next world. She shares a lot with Hathor, so labels sometimes use both names. The head is carved wood covered in gold, with dark horns and inlaid eyes, and it was found in the Treasury, the small room beyond the burial chamber. Almost all of Tutankhamun's treasure went to Cairo and is now gathered at the Grand Egyptian Museum, which you visited on the 11th. A few pieces were kept here in Luxor, near the tomb, though some may have moved, so if the cow is not on display she is probably in Giza. If she is here, look at her horns: they curve like a lyre, a cradle for the sun.

period: Ahmose I, mid-16th century BC; Ramesses I, c. 1292-1290 BC
summary: The founder of the New Kingdom and the founder of the Ramesside line lie here, one of them after more than 130 years in a curiosity museum at Niagara Falls.
look: In the newer wing devoted to the armies of the early New Kingdom, a dim room holds two royal mummies in glass cases. Keep your voice low. Around them in the wing: chariots, weapons and the story of the war against the Hyksos.
story:
Ahmose I finished the war that his predecessors Seqenenre and Kamose had begun against the Hyksos, foreign kings who ruled the north from Avaris. He attacked Avaris several times before it fell, then besieged Sharuhen near Gaza for three years, reunited Egypt and opened the New Kingdom. His mummy was found in 1881 in the royal cache at Deir el-Bahari, in a coffin bearing his name, and unwrapped by Gaston Maspero in 1887. The identification is not certain: in 1980 James Harris and Edward Wente questioned it, partly because the arms are not crossed over the chest.

The second mummy has a stranger story. Members of the Abd el-Rassul family, who had found the same cache, took it out, and around 1860 it was sold in Luxor to a Canadian doctor, James Douglas. It ended up in the Niagara Falls Museum, where it stayed for more than 130 years. In 1999 the collection was sold to the Michael C. Carlos Museum in Atlanta. CT scans, X-rays and radiocarbon dating, the arms crossed high on the chest, and a family resemblance convinced researchers that this was most likely Ramesses I, founder of the 19th Dynasty and grandfather of Ramesses II. On 24 October 2003 he returned to Egypt with full official honours.
details: Ahmose's arms lie at his sides, not crossed: one reason some experts doubt the identification.
Ramesses I's arms are crossed high on the chest, a royal pose that helped identify him.
Around the wing: chariots and weapons of the army that drove out the Hyksos.
Ramesses I reigned only about two years; his small tomb, KV16, was finished in a hurry.
fun_fact: Ramesses I was buried around 1290 BC and came home on 24 October 2003, after more than a century as an anonymous exhibit at Niagara Falls.
narration: In this dim room lie two kings who each founded something. The first is Ahmose the First, who finished the war against the Hyksos, the foreign rulers of northern Egypt. He besieged their capital Avaris until it fell, chased them to Sharuhen near Gaza, reunited the country and opened the New Kingdom, more than 3,500 years ago. His mummy was found in 1881 in the great royal cache at Deir el-Bahari. Some experts doubt it is really him, partly because the arms are not crossed on the chest. The second has a wilder story. Around 1860, a mummy taken from the same cache was sold in Luxor to a Canadian doctor and ended up in a curiosity museum at Niagara Falls, where it stayed for more than 130 years. In 1999 a museum in Atlanta bought the collection. Scans, radiocarbon dates and a family likeness convinced researchers that this was most likely Ramesses the First, grandfather of Ramesses the Second. In October 2003 he came home with full honours. Look at his arms, crossed high on the chest, the pose of a king.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, reign of Amenhotep III, c. 1390-1352 BC
summary: A commoner from the Delta who became Amenhotep III's master of works, got a temple next to the king's, and was prayed to as a healer a thousand years later.
look: A granodiorite statue about 1.3 m high, from Karnak: a man seated cross-legged as a scribe, a papyrus open across his lap. Look at the soft rolls of fat on his chest and belly: in Egyptian art, the mark of a successful, well-fed official.
story:
Amenhotep son of Hapu was born around 1425 BC at Athribis in the Delta, son of Hapu and Itu, with no royal blood. He rose late, in middle age, under Amenhotep III: Scribe of Recruits, organising manpower for the king's projects, then overseer of works. He supervised the king's huge mortuary temple on the west bank, of which only the Colossi of Memnon remain, and took part in the king's first jubilee in year 30.

His reward was extraordinary: his own mortuary temple beside the king's, the only private cult temple among the royal ones. His statues stood at Karnak, where people approached him as an intermediary with Amun. On one of them, now in Cairo, he says he has reached 80 years and hopes to reach 110, the ideal lifespan of Egyptian wisdom literature.

After his death he became a sage and a healer. In Ptolemaic times he had chapels at Deir el-Medina and in Hatshepsut's temple at Deir el-Bahari, where he was honoured with Imhotep, the builder of the Step Pyramid. Greek-speaking pilgrims called him Amenothes.
details: The rolls of fat on his chest: not an insult but a boast. Only a rich man ate well enough to have them.
The papyrus across his lap, the badge of a scribe: literacy was the key to his whole career.
The cross-legged scribe pose echoes Old Kingdom scribe statues, chosen to look wise and traditional.
His mortuary temple stood beside Amenhotep III's on the west bank, near the Colossi of Memnon you saw on the 21st.
fun_fact: His mortuary temple carried a long, detailed curse against anyone who disturbed or robbed it.
narration: This seated scribe is Amenhotep son of Hapu, one of the very few ordinary Egyptians who became a god. He was born about 1425 BC at Athribis in the Delta, son of a man called Hapu, with no royal blood. He rose late, in middle age, under King Amenhotep the Third: first as scribe of recruits, organising the workforce, then as the king's master of works. He supervised the king's vast temple on the west bank, of which only the Colossi of Memnon remain; you passed them on the 21st. His reward was unheard of: his own mortuary temple, built next to the king's. His statues stood at Karnak, where people asked him to pass their prayers on to Amun. On one, now in Cairo, he says he has reached 80 years and hopes to reach 110, the perfect lifespan. After his death he became a healer and a sage. Over a thousand years later, in Ptolemaic times, the sick still came to him at Deir el-Bahari, together with Imhotep. Look at the rolls of fat on his chest: here, that means success.

period: Middle Kingdom, 12th Dynasty, Senusret III, c. 1878-1839 BC
summary: A king who chose to look tired: Senusret III's heavy-lidded, careworn face is one of the most human portraits in Egyptian art.
look: A red granite head of Senusret III with deep-set eyes, heavy lids, pouches beneath them, a downturned mouth and big ears turned forward. Follow the labels to find it, then compare it with the smooth, smiling New Kingdom faces around the museum.
story:
Senusret III ruled from about 1878 to 1839 BC and pushed Egypt's border deep into Nubia. He campaigned there in his years 8, 10, 16 and 19, cleared a navigable canal through the First Cataract at Aswan, and built a chain of forts at the Second Cataract, Buhen, Semna, Uronarti and others, now under Lake Nasser. His boundary stela at Semna tells his successors that a son who keeps the border is his true son.

His sculptors broke with tradition. Instead of an ageless mask, they gave him hollow eyes, heavy lids and a weary mouth on a young, muscular body. Some read it as a ruler burdened by care; others as a stern king meant to be feared. He was worshipped as a god in Nubia long after his death.
details: The eyes: deep sockets, heavy upper lids and pouches below. No earlier king was carved like this.
The ears: big and set forward, perhaps a king who hears everything.
Find a New Kingdom face nearby and compare: the 12th Dynasty frown against the 18th Dynasty smile.
fun_fact: Herodotus tells of Sesostris, a pharaoh who conquered half the world; that Greek legend is partly built on memories of this king.
narration: This red granite head belongs to Senusret the Third, a king of the Middle Kingdom who ruled about 1850 BC. Look at the face: deep-set eyes, heavy lids, pouches beneath them, a mouth that turns down, and big ears pushed forward. Earlier kings had smooth, ageless faces. Senusret chose to look tired. Some see a ruler weighed down by care for his people, others a stern king who sees and hears everything. He pushed Egypt's border deep into Nubia and built forts at the Second Cataract that now lie under Lake Nasser. Herodotus tells of a conquering pharaoh called Sesostris, a legend partly built on his memory. Now compare his eyes with any smiling New Kingdom face nearby.

summary: A small, cool museum on the Corniche that explains step by step how the Egyptians turned a body into a mummy, with the real materials, tools and a high priest.
look: On the Corniche in front of the Mina Palace Hotel, north of Luxor Temple, facing the Nile. A corridor with ten panels copied from the Book of the Dead papyri of Ani and Hunefer leads into one dim hall with 19 cases and over 60 objects. Allow 30 to 45 minutes.
story:
President Hosni Mubarak opened the museum in 1997 in a former visitor centre. It is small, 2,035 square metres including a lecture hall and a video room, and that is its strength: everything is about one subject.

The corridor at the start sets the scene with copies of vignettes from the papyri of Ani and Hunefer, both in the British Museum, following a burial from death to tomb. Then the cases are arranged by theme: the gods of embalming, the materials (natron, organic materials, embalming fluid), the tools, canopic jars, shabtis, amulets, the coffin of a man called Padiamun, the mummy of Masaharta, a High Priest of Amun around 1050 BC, and mummified animals.

After yesterday's tombs on the West Bank, this is where it all makes sense: the jackal-headed Anubis leaning over a mummy, the four jars by the coffin, the priest with the adze at the tomb door.
details: Canopic jars with lids shaped as the four sons of Horus: human, baboon, jackal and falcon.
The mummy of Masaharta, High Priest of Amun about 1050 BC, son of the priest-king Pinedjem I.
The coffin of Padiamun: painted wood covered with protective gods and texts.
Mummified animals: cats, fish and a crocodile among them.
The amulet case: small charms that were tucked between the bandages, each with a job.
fun_fact: The whole process took about 70 days, which the Egyptians linked to the time the star Sirius stays hidden from the sky each year.
narration: This small museum on the Corniche explains one thing: how the Egyptians made a mummy. It opened in 1997 and fits into a single dim, cool hall. The corridor at the start shows scenes copied from two famous Book of the Dead papyri, those of Ani and Hunefer, following a funeral from death to the tomb. Then come the cases, arranged like a lesson. The gods of embalming, with Anubis the jackal in charge. The materials: natron salt to dry the body, resins, oils and linen. The tools. The canopic jars that held the organs, with lids shaped as the four sons of Horus. The amulets tucked between the bandages, and the little shabti figures that worked for the dead. At the heart of the room lies a real person: Masaharta, High Priest of Amun about 1050 BC, son of the priest-king Pinedjem, whose name you saw on the colossus at Karnak. There is a painted coffin of a man called Padiamun, and mummified animals: cats, fish, a crocodile. The whole process took about 70 days. Start at the canopic jars: a human head, a baboon, a jackal and a falcon.

period: Third Intermediate Period, 21st Dynasty, High Priest c. 1054-1045 BC
summary: Son of a priest-king and brother of a pharaoh, Masaharta ran Thebes for Amun, and his family were the ones who hid Egypt's royal mummies.
look: The mummy of Masaharta, High Priest of Amun, in its own case at the heart of the hall. He died around 3,000 years ago. The painted coffin nearby belongs to a different man, Padiamun; read the labels so you do not mix them up.
story:
Masaharta was High Priest of Amun at Thebes from about 1054 to 1045 BC. His father was Pinedjem I, the high priest who ruled Upper Egypt and in 1054 BC declared himself king; Pinedjem's name is carved on the colossus at Karnak's second pylon. His mother was probably Duathathor-Henuttawy, a daughter of Ramesses XI, the last Ramesside. His brother Psusennes I became pharaoh at Tanis in the Delta, and another brother, Menkheperre, later held the high priesthood. His sister Maatkare was probably God's Wife of Amun. It was a family business: the north had the crown, the south had the god.

These priest-kings also managed the royal dead. Robbers had plundered the Valley of the Kings, so the priests gathered the kings' mummies, rewrapped them and moved them into hiding; many scholars think much of the old gold went back into circulation along the way. Masaharta himself restored the mummy of Amenhotep I, in year 16 of King Smendes. In the end his own body was found with members of his family in the royal cache at Deir el-Bahari, DB320, discovered in 1881. It was later moved from the Egyptian Museum in Cairo to this museum.
details: The mummy itself: a High Priest of Amun from the family that hid Egypt's royal mummies.
The coffin of Padiamun nearby is a different man's; a good example of a painted wooden coffin.
Pinedjem I, his father, is the name carved on the colossus in front of Karnak's second pylon.
His brother Psusennes I was buried at Tanis in a silver coffin with a gold mask, one of Egypt's great treasures.
fun_fact: His family ran both ends of Egypt: one brother was pharaoh in the Delta, another succeeded to the high priesthood at Thebes, and a sister was God's Wife of Amun.
narration: Here lies Masaharta, High Priest of Amun at Thebes about 3,000 years ago. Picture Egypt split in two. In the north a king ruled from the Delta. In the south the High Priests of Amun ruled Thebes in the god's name. Masaharta's father was Pinedjem, the high priest who declared himself king; you saw his name carved on the colossus at Karnak's second pylon. His mother was probably a daughter of Ramesses the Eleventh, the last of the Ramesside kings. His brother Psusennes became pharaoh in the north and was buried at Tanis in a silver coffin. These priest-kings also looked after the royal dead. Robbers had plundered the Valley of the Kings, so the priests rewrapped the royal mummies and moved them into hiding, and many scholars think much of the kings' gold went back into circulation on the way. Masaharta himself restored the mummy of Amenhotep the First. In the end his own body lay in the great hiding place at Deir el-Bahari, found in 1881. Look closely at him: this was a member of Egypt's ruling family.

period: Mostly Late Period to Roman times
summary: Cats, crocodiles and fish: the Egyptians mummified millions of animals, as pets, food, sacred beasts and offerings, and plenty of them were fakes.
look: A few cases of animal mummies, including cats, fish and a crocodile. Look at the shapes of the wrappings: some follow the animal's body, others are neat geometric parcels. The labels say what each one was for.
story:
Most animal mummies fall into four groups. Pets, buried to keep their owners company: cats, dogs, monkeys, gazelles. Food, the 'victual mummies' of meat and ducks for the dead to eat; Tutankhamun had boxes of them. Sacred animals, a single chosen creature that lived in a temple as the god's living image, like the Apis bull at Memphis or the rams of Khnum at Elephantine, pampered in life and buried with honours. And above all votive offerings: pilgrims bought a mummified animal at a temple and dedicated it to the god.

That last trade became an industry in the Late Period and under the Ptolemies and Romans. Animals were raised on temple grounds for it. About four million ibises, Thoth's bird, were buried at Tuna el-Gebel. Cats went to Bastet, crocodiles to Sobek, Nile perch to the goddess Neith near Esna. Quality fell as demand rose: scans show many bundles hold only a few bones, feathers or reeds. The pilgrim never knew.

Modern people were not kinder. In 1888 a farmer found a vast cat cemetery in Middle Egypt, and around 1890 some 19 tons of cat mummies were shipped to Liverpool and sold as fertiliser.
details: The cat: look at the wrapping pattern. The best cat mummies have geometric bands and modelled ears.
The crocodile: Sobek's animal. You met his sacred crocodiles at Kom Ombo on the 20th.
The fish: Nile perch were sacred to Neith, and thousands were buried near Esna, which you visited on the 20th.
Think about what is inside: the label may say whether scans found a whole animal or only fragments.
fun_fact: Many votive mummies were fakes: scans show bundles holding a few bones, feathers or reeds, sold to pilgrims who never knew the difference.
narration: These are the animals. The Egyptians mummified millions of them, for four reasons. Some were pets, buried to keep their owners company. Some were food for the dead. Some were sacred animals, a single chosen creature that lived in a temple as the living image of a god, like the Apis bull at Memphis or the ram of Khnum at Elephantine. But most were offerings. A pilgrim bought a mummified animal at the temple and gave it to the god, the way you might light a candle. Under the last pharaohs, the Ptolemies and the Romans, it became an industry, with animals raised on temple grounds. About four million ibises, the bird of Thoth, were buried at Tuna el-Gebel. Cats went to Bastet, crocodiles to Sobek, Nile perch to the goddess Neith near Esna. Quality fell as demand grew, and scans show that many bundles hold only a few bones, feathers or reeds. Modern people were worse: around 1890 a ship carried tons of cat mummies to Liverpool to be sold as fertiliser. Find the cat, and look at the neat pattern of its wrapping.

summary: Hooks, natron, resin and amulets: the 70-day recipe for eternity, as a Greek tourist described it 2,500 years ago and as the embalmers' own pots confirm.
look: Cases of embalming materials and tools: natron, resins and oils, linen, instruments, canopic jars and amulets. Read them as a sequence: drying, emptying, filling, wrapping, protecting. The amulets show the charms that went between the bandages.
story:
The Greek historian Herodotus, writing around 450 BC, describes three price levels. The best: the brain drawn out through the nose with an iron hook, the belly opened along the flank with a sharp Ethiopian stone, the cavity rinsed with palm wine and spices, and the body laid in natron for 70 days. The middle: cedar oil injected to dissolve the organs, drained after the natron. The cheapest: a purge and the natron. Modern study adds that the brain was often liquefied with a rod, and the drying took about 40 days of the 70.

The body was washed in a purification tent, the ibu, and worked on in the 'House of Beauty'. Lungs, liver, stomach and intestines went into canopic jars protected by the four sons of Horus. The heart stayed, to be weighed against the feather of Maat. Over it lay a heart scarab with a spell asking the heart not to testify against its owner. Then came oils, resin and many layers of linen, with amulets between them.

Last came the Opening of the Mouth: a priest touched the mummy's mouth with an adze so the dead could breathe and speak. Pots from a 26th Dynasty embalming workshop at Saqqara still held residues of cedar, juniper, Dead Sea bitumen, beeswax and imported resins.
details: Natron: a natural mix of salts from desert lakes such as the Wadi Natrun, packed in and around the body.
Canopic lids: human Imsety for the liver, baboon Hapy for the lungs, jackal Duamutef for the stomach, falcon Qebehsenuef for the gut.
Amulets: the djed pillar for stability, the Eye of Horus for healing, the heart scarab over the heart.
Resin: the dark, glassy coating that sealed the wrappings and made many old mummies look black.
fun_fact: The Greek historian Diodorus says the man who made the first cut was chased away with stones and curses, because wounding a body was an offence, even when it was your job.
narration: Here is the embalmer's kit, and the recipe for eternity. The Greek historian Herodotus described it around 450 BC, with three price levels. In the best, the brain was drawn out through the nose with a hook, the belly was cut open on the left side with a sharp stone blade, the cavity rinsed with palm wine and spices, and the body buried in natron, a natural salt from the desert lakes. Modern studies show the drying took about 40 days, inside a 70-day ritual. Lungs, liver, stomach and intestines went into four canopic jars. The heart stayed in the body, because it would be weighed in the judgment of the dead. Over it lay a heart scarab with a spell asking the heart not to testify against its owner. Then came oils, resin and many layers of linen, with amulets tucked between them while a priest recited spells. Last, the Opening of the Mouth: a priest touched the mummy's lips with an adze, so the dead could breathe and speak again. Look for the natron in its case: plain whitish salt, the most important ingredient of all.

period: Papyrus used from at least c. 2560 BC; modern craft revived in 1962
summary: Real papyrus is a woven sheet of plant pith you can see through; the cheap stuff is often banana leaf. Here is how to tell, and how to bargain.
look: Hold the sheet up to the light. Real papyrus shows a criss-cross of strips, darker lines where they overlap, running one way on the front and the other way behind. Banana-leaf fakes look uniform, with veins in one direction only, and feel soft and floppy.
story:
Papyrus, Cyperus papyrus, is a tall sedge that once filled the Delta marshes. To make a sheet, the Egyptians peeled the stem, cut the white pith into strips about 40 cm long, laid one layer side by side and a second across it at right angles, then hammered and pressed them while moist and dried them under pressure. Polished sheets were glued into rolls. The oldest inscribed papyri yet found, the Diary of Merer from Wadi al-Jarf, date to about 2560 BC and describe moving stone for the Great Pyramid.

Our words come through Greek: papyros gave 'paper', and byblos, named after the Phoenician port of Byblos, gave 'Bible'.

By the late 1700s the plant had died out in Egypt. The modern craft was revived in 1962 by Hassan Ragab, an Egyptian engineer and diplomat, and today's 'papyrus institutes' grew from his work. The demonstration you will be shown, slicing, soaking and pressing, is real. So is the sales pitch afterwards.

On price: hand-painted work on real papyrus costs more than a print, and the first price is high. Decide what you would pay before you ask, offer about a third, settle somewhere in the middle, and walk away smiling if it does not work.
details: Light test: hold it up. Real papyrus shows a criss-cross grid of strips; banana leaf shows parallel veins only.
Roll test: real papyrus rolls gently without cracking; banana leaf is brittle and splits along its veins.
Paint test: hand-painted work shows brush marks and uneven colour; prints are flat and perfect.
Your name in a cartouche is fun, but agree the price, name included, before anyone starts painting.
Opening offer: about a third of the first price is normal. Meet in the middle and part friends either way.
fun_fact: The words paper and Bible both come from papyrus: paper from the Greek papyros, Bible from byblos, the name of the Phoenician port it was traded through.
narration: A quick guide before you buy papyrus. Real papyrus is made from the pith of a tall marsh plant. The stem is peeled, the white pith cut into strips, one layer laid across another at right angles, then pressed and dried. So hold a sheet up to the light. Real papyrus shows a criss-cross grid of strips, darker where they overlap. Fakes made of banana leaf look even, with veins running one way only, and they feel soft. Roll it gently: real papyrus bends without cracking, banana leaf splits. Look at the paint: hand-painted work shows brush marks and uneven colour, prints are flat and perfect. The oldest written rolls, about 4,500 years old, record the building of the Great Pyramid. The plant died out in Egypt, and an engineer called Hassan Ragab revived the craft in 1962. The shop demonstration is real; so is the sales pitch. Offer about a third of the first price, settle in the middle, and smile. The word paper, and even the word Bible, come from Greek names for papyrus. Now hold a sheet up to the light, and look for the grid.

period: New Kingdom and later, from the 18th Dynasty, c. 1500 BC
summary: Once a year Amun left Karnak in his golden boat and travelled to Luxor to renew the king's divine power, and the city celebrated for weeks.
look: Nothing single to look at: this festival is the reason Luxor Temple and the Avenue of Sphinxes exist. Its best picture is the procession carved in the Colonnade of Amenhotep III at Luxor Temple, and the barque scenes on Hatshepsut's Red Chapel at Karnak. Walk any stretch of the Avenue of Sphinxes and you are on the route.
story:
Opet was celebrated in the second month of Akhet, the flood season, roughly the time of year you are travelling. Under Thutmose III it lasted 11 days; by the start of Ramesses III's reign it had stretched to 24, and by his death to 27.

Priests lifted the barques of the Theban triad, Amun, his wife Mut and their son Khonsu, gilded boats with a veiled shrine in the middle, onto their shoulders and carried them out of Karnak. Some years they went by land along the Avenue of Sphinxes; other years the god sailed in his great river barge, Userhat-Amun, 'mighty of prow is Amun', built of Lebanese cedar covered in gold, with ram heads at prow and stern. Soldiers, musicians, dancers and acrobats went with them, and officials from all over the country helped run it.

At Luxor Temple the king met the god in the inner rooms. In a ritual of union and rebirth he was renewed as the son of Amun and recrowned, his royal ka, the divine power of kingship, refreshed for another year. Then the gods returned to Karnak.

Ordinary people did not enter the sanctuary. They watched from the route and the riverbanks, shared in bread and beer, and could put questions to the god as the barque passed. Today the moulid of Sheikh Yusuf Abu el-Haggag, whose boat is carried around Luxor, is widely seen as a distant echo of Opet.
details: Luxor Temple colonnade: the full procession, barques, soldiers, acrobats and musicians, carved under Tutankhamun.
The Avenue of Sphinxes: the land route of the procession between Karnak and Luxor Temple.
Red Chapel at Karnak: Hatshepsut's version, with the barque carried on poles by priests.
Spot Amun's barque in any relief: a boat with a ram's head at prow and stern and a veiled cabin in the middle.
The Abu el-Haggag mosque on top of Luxor Temple: its saint's moulid parades a boat through town.
fun_fact: Oracle questions were answered by the barque itself: Egyptologists think a lurch forward on the priests' shoulders meant yes, a step back meant no.
narration: Imagine Thebes in the flood season, around this time of year, more than 3,000 years ago. The Opet Festival has begun. At Karnak, priests lift the sacred boats of the gods onto their shoulders: Amun, his wife Mut and their son Khonsu, each in a gilded barque with a veiled shrine in the middle. Some years they carried them along the Avenue of Sphinxes to Luxor Temple. Other years Amun sailed upriver in his great river barge, Userhat Amun, mighty of prow is Amun, built of Lebanese cedar covered in gold, with ram heads at each end. Soldiers marched, musicians played, acrobats bent over backwards. At Luxor Temple, in the inner rooms, the king met the god. In a ritual of union and rebirth he was renewed as Amun's son, and his royal power, his ka, was refreshed for another year. Then the gods went home. Under Thutmose the Third the festival lasted 11 days. Under Ramesses the Third it stretched to 27. Ordinary people never entered the sanctuary, but they lined the route, shared bread and beer, and could ask the god questions; a lurch of the barque on the priests' shoulders was an answer. Today the moulid of Abu el-Haggag, whose boat is carried around Luxor, may be its distant echo. Walk a stretch of the Avenue of Sphinxes, and you are on the route.
